match.reason: No bank point teaches inverse functions: the closest matches cover relations, function notation, differentiability and logarithms, which are related but not the same idea as reversing a function by swapping x and y.

draft.title: Inverse functions
card: The inverse of f, written f⁻¹, reverses f. If f takes 2 to 7, then f⁻¹ takes 7 back to 2.
To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, then solve for y. Example: f(x) = 2x + 3. Write y = 2x + 3, swap to x = 2y + 3, so y = (x − 3)/2. This gives f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

An inverse exists only if f is one-to-one: each output comes from exactly one input. A horizontal line must cut the graph at most once. So y = x² on all of R has no inverse, because 2 and −2 both give 4.
The graph of f⁻¹ is the graph of f reflected in the line y = x. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f.
draft.remember: Swap x and y to reverse a function. Only a one-to-one function has an inverse.

a.q: What is the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 6?
a.why: Swap to x = 3y − 6, so 3y = x + 6 and y = (x + 6)/3. Check: f(3) = 3, and f⁻¹(3) = 3 gives back 3. The option (x − 6)/3 has a sign error when moving the 6 across.
a.clue: Swap x and y first, then undo the subtraction before the multiplication.

b.q: Which function has an inverse that is also a function, with its rule defined on the whole domain given?
opts: f(x) = x², for x in R
f(x) = 4 − x², for x in R
b.why: Only f(x) = 2x + 1 is one-to-one, so any horizontal line cuts it once. The other three each give the same output for x and −x, so a horizontal line cuts them twice. Having a rule that can be rearranged does not make a function one-to-one.
b.clue: Does any output come from two different inputs, such as 2 and −2?

problems.detail: The stem 'has an inverse that is also a function, with its rule defined on the whole domain given' is awkward and confusing. It also suggests an inverse might exist without being a function, which clashes with the card's statement that an inverse exists only when f is one-to-one. A simpler stem would be clearer: 'Which function, on the domain given, has an inverse function?'

check.summary: Both answers check out: (x + 6)/3 for a and 2x + 1 for b. The only issue is that question b's stem is awkwardly worded and implies inverses can exist without being functions, which the card does not teach.

final.title: Inverse functions
card: The inverse of \(f\), written \(f^{-1}\), reverses \(f\). If \(f\) takes 2 to 7, then \(f^{-1}\) takes 7 back to 2.

To find it, write \(y = f(x)\), swap \(x\) and \(y\), then solve for \(y\). Example: \(f(x) = 2x + 3\). Write \(y = 2x + 3\), swap to \(x = 2y + 3\), so \(y = \frac{x - 3}{2}\). This gives \(f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 3}{2}\).

An inverse exists only if \(f\) is one-to-one: each output comes from exactly one input. A horizontal line must cut the graph at most once. So \(y = x^{2}\) on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) has no inverse, because 2 and \(-2\) both give 4.
The graph of \(f^{-1}\) is the graph of \(f\) reflected in the line \(y = x\). The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\).

3.alt: The parabola \(y = x^{2}\) and the horizontal line \(y = 4\). The line cuts the parabola twice, at \((-2, 4)\) and \((2, 4)\), so \(y = x^{2}\) is not one-to-one and has no inverse.

4.alt: The line \(y = f(x) = 2x + 3\) and its inverse \(y = f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 3}{2}\), reflections of each other in the dotted line \(y = x\). All four quadrants show, and both lines run on past the axes. The point \((0, 3)\) on \(f\) matches \((3, 0)\) on \(f^{-1}\).

a.clue: Swap \(x\) and \(y\) first, then undo the subtraction before the multiplication.
